source.title: Understanding Why Neural Networks Generalize Well Through GSNR of Parameters
source.authors: Jinlong Liu; Guo-qing Jiang; Yunzhi Bai; Ting Chen; Huayan Wang

record.file_problem: The full paper text, including appendices, is present. Some figure values are not available as text.
record.tranche_reason: The study derives and empirically evaluates a GSNR-based measure of one-step generalization ratio, a different measure aimed at explaining generalization gaps.
record.gate_note: The paper reports GSNR–OSGR comparisons. It does not report held-out accuracy for natural versus randomized labels; its statement that both training losses reach zero is not a test of held-out generalization. Figure-only correlation values are not reconstructed.
record.test_reason: The study tests a GSNR-based estimate of one-step generalization ratio, which none of V1–V8 names. It reports zero training loss with real and randomized labels but no corresponding held-out accuracy comparison required by V1. Its width variations do not establish test-error behavior beyond interpolation, and GSNR is not V7's magnitude-aware sharpness.
record.authors_conclusion: The record accurately paraphrases the authors' conclusion: they argue that larger parameter GSNR leads to smaller generalization gaps and that gradient descent raises GSNR through feature learning. Their quantitative derivation relies on small learning rates and a non-overfitting approximation; the reported empirical validation primarily concerns OSGR rather than final held-out accuracy.
record.recipe_differences: The study analyzes parameter GSNR and a derived one-step generalization ratio; it does not reproduce the claim versions' interventions or measures.
record.method_sensitivity: The empirical relationship becomes more scattered as training proceeds; on CIFAR10, batch normalization is reported as a possible reason the estimates do not lie perfectly on the diagonal. The reported positive correlation persists until convergence begins.

fits_no_version.finding: Empirical OSGR correlates with its GSNR-based estimate across MNIST, CIFAR-10, and synthetic regression settings. Agreement becomes more scattered during training; CIFAR-10 shows imperfect early agreement, potentially related to batch normalization.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: A GSNR-based expression predicts one-step generalization ratio approximately, with agreement depending on training stage and model setting.

fits_no_version.finding: Section 3.1 reports rising early GSNR with real labels and persistently low GSNR with randomized labels, although both training losses reach zero. No corresponding held-out accuracy comparison is reported.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: GSNR trajectories distinguish real-label learning from random-label memorization despite both achieving zero training loss.

record.problems: The analysis relies on a stated non-overfitting limit approximation that the authors say becomes less valid as training proceeds. Empirical comparisons are presented mainly in figures without exact text values. The CIFAR10 comparison is less closely aligned, and the authors suggest batch-normalization running statistics may affect the estimate.
record.rows_left_out: No additional distinct generalization-gap results were stated in text. Figure 4 reports GSNR trajectories for real and randomized labels and says both training losses reach zero, but does not report held-out error; it therefore does not provide a result on the claim's natural-label test-generalization outcome.

untested.parts: Natural-label held-out accuracy above chance and random-label held-out accuracy at chance under the same recipe; zero training loss alone does not establish coexistence.
Test error as width increases beyond the width needed for zero training error.
Convolutional versus fully connected held-out performance and the contribution of local connectivity.
Adaptive optimizers versus SGD under specified tuning budgets.
Batch-size effects on held-out performance under fixed epoch budgets and adapted recipes.
Dropout interventions and their effects on held-out error.
Magnitude-aware sharpness versus generalization gaps and its ranking against norm- and margin-based measures.
Retraining after removing memorized examples versus equally many random examples.

record.verdict_notes: No verdicts apply to V1–V8. The paper's own GSNR experiments go beyond citation alone, but address a different proposed explanation of generalization.

versions.untested_parts: No held-out accuracy or test error comparison for natural versus randomized labels is reported.
No width sweep measuring test error beyond the interpolation threshold is reported.
No convolutional versus fully connected test-error comparison is reported.
No adaptive optimizer versus SGD held-out performance comparison is reported.
No batch-size comparison of held-out performance is reported.
No dropout intervention or held-out error comparison is reported.
The study examines GSNR in relation to OSGR, not magnitude-aware sharpness or its ranking against norm- and margin-based measures.
No memorized-example removal experiment is reported.

rows.subject: simple CNN structure consists of 2 Conv-Relu-MaxPooling blocks and 2 fully-connected layers
rows.operation_detail: Compared empirical OSGR with OSGR estimated as a function of GSNR across training sets and model settings.
rows.measure: Correlation between empirical OSGR and the GSNR-based estimate; text says correlation remains high through convergence at epoch 2,500.
rows.note: The text describes points as closely distributed along the equality line early in training and says correlation remains high at convergence; exact plotted values are not stated.
rows.check: The reported high correlation concerns empirical versus estimated OSGR, not any claim version. The correlation is qualitatively observed, but cannot establish a version's effect.

rows.subject: deeper network on CIFAR10, consisting of 4 Conv-BN-Relu-Conv-BN-Relu-MaxPooling blocks and 3 fully-connected layers
rows.operation_detail: Compared empirical OSGR with the GSNR-based estimate across training sets, label-noise settings, and channel counts.
rows.measure: Correlation between empirical OSGR and the GSNR-based estimate; text reports strong positive correlation until training begins to converge.
rows.note: The text says the points do not perfectly lie on the diagonal early in training and attributes possible influence to batch-normalization running statistics; positive correlation remains until convergence begins.
rows.check: Imperfect agreement and positive correlation concern the GSNR-based OSGR estimate. They do not constitute partial evidence for any claim version.

rows.subject: two-layer regression model with FC-ReLU structure
rows.size_stated: 2 inputs, 1 hidden layer with N neurons; N ∈ {6, 8, 10, 12, 14, 16, 18, 20}
rows.operation_detail: Compared empirical OSGR with the GSNR-based estimate across training-set sizes, noise levels, and hidden-layer sizes.
rows.measure: Correlation between empirical OSGR and the GSNR-based estimate; text reports close agreement early and high correlation through convergence, while the GSNR-based estimate decreases significantly.
rows.note: The paper describes the relation qualitatively; exact plotted values are not stated.
rows.check: The regression experiment measures agreement between empirical and estimated OSGR, not any claim version; varying hidden width does not itself test V2.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

relation.reason: The paper discusses memorization and generalization while developing a GSNR-based explanation; it neither tests a listed version nor uses its finding as a tool.

tranche.reason: The experiments measure GSNR and agreement between empirical and estimated OSGR, which do not test V1–V8. Width variation does not establish post-interpolation test-error behavior; fitting original and randomized labels does not supply V1's held-out accuracy comparison.

source_check.notes: The authors' conclusion is accurately paraphrased. The quantitative derivation assumes small learning rates and a non-overfitting approximation; the three rows report qualitative OSGR agreement without numerical correlation coefficients.
